document.subtitle: Comprehensive Medical Reference and Review for the MCCQE, 41st edition

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman is prescribed codeine after a dental extraction and reports no analgesic benefit at a standard dose. She recalls that tramadol was similarly ineffective after a previous procedure. She takes no interacting medications, has normal renal and hepatic function, and denies substance use. What is the most likely explanation for her lack of response?

options.text: She carries nonfunctional CYP2D6 alleles and cannot activate the prodrug to morphine
She carries hypermorphic CYP2D6 alleles giving an ultra-rapid metabolizer phenotype
She carries CYP2C9 loss-of-function alleles
Her intestinal first-pass metabolism of codeine is reduced
Phase II glucuronidation is producing an inactive metabolite instead of an active one

questions.explanation: Genetic polymorphisms of metabolizing enzymes alter drug response, and tamoxifen, tramadol, and codeine are prodrugs activated by CYP2D6; nonfunctional alleles reduce effectiveness. Codeine must be biotransformed to morphine to produce analgesia, so a patient who cannot perform this activation step will get no benefit from either codeine or tramadol at normal doses.

optionExplanations.b: Hypermorphic CYP2D6 alleles produce an ultra-rapid metabolizer phenotype, which would accelerate conversion to morphine rather than prevent analgesia.
optionExplanations.c: CYP2C9 loss-of-function alleles affect warfarin, leading to higher drug concentrations, greater effect, and lower dose requirements.
optionExplanations.d: Reduced first-pass metabolism would increase, not decrease, systemic exposure to the drug.
optionExplanations.e: Phase II conjugation of morphine can itself yield biologically active metabolites such as morphine glucuronide, so this does not explain complete lack of effect.

questions.question: A 61-year-old man has taken simvastatin uneventfully for two years. On the advice of a friend he begins drinking a large glass of grapefruit juice every morning. Two weeks later he develops diffuse muscle aching and weakness, and his simvastatin plasma concentration is found to be markedly higher than previously. Which mechanism best explains this interaction?

options.text: Inhibition of intestinal CYP3A4, markedly reducing first-pass metabolism
Induction of hepatic CYP3A4, increasing simvastatin clearance
Induction of P-glycoprotein, increasing efflux of simvastatin
Displacement of simvastatin from albumin binding sites
Inhibition of renal tubular secretion of simvastatin

questions.explanation: Grapefruit juice is a potent inhibitor of intestinal CYP3A4, resulting in markedly reduced first-pass metabolism and numerous drug interactions; simvastatin AUC has been reported to increase 17-fold. CYP inhibition leads to an increased concentration and bioavailability of the substrate drug, which accounts for the rise in simvastatin exposure and the muscle symptoms in this patient.

optionExplanations.b: Enzyme induction increases metabolizing enzyme activity and would lower, not raise, simvastatin concentrations.
optionExplanations.c: P-glycoprotein inducers such as rifampin and St. John's wort increase efflux activity and decrease serum concentrations of substrates.
optionExplanations.d: Displacement from plasma proteins increases the free fraction, which is often cleared with no harmful effect, and is not the described grapefruit mechanism.
optionExplanations.e: Grapefruit juice acts on presystemic intestinal metabolism rather than on renal tubular secretion.

source.reference: CP6 — Factors Affecting Drug Biotransformation: Enzyme Inhibition

questions.question: A 52-year-old man who has consumed large amounts of alcohol daily for many years takes acetaminophen at recommended doses for several days for back pain. He presents with nausea, right upper quadrant discomfort, and markedly elevated transaminases. Which mechanism best explains his increased susceptibility to hepatocellular damage?

options.text: Chronic alcohol consumption induces CYP2E1, increasing production of the toxic metabolite NAPQI
Acute alcohol ingestion inhibits CYP2E1, causing accumulation of unchanged acetaminophen
Alcohol induces CYP1A2, accelerating conversion of acetaminophen to morphine-like metabolites
Alcohol induces P-glycoprotein, increasing hepatic uptake of acetaminophen
Alcohol saturates glomerular filtration of acetaminophen, prolonging its half-life

questions.explanation: Biotransformation can convert a drug to a toxic metabolite, and acetaminophen is converted to NAPQI. Alcohol has varying effects on metabolism: acute ingestion inhibits CYP2E1, whereas chronic consumption induces CYP2E1, increasing the risk of hepatocellular damage from acetaminophen by increasing production of the toxic metabolite NAPQI. This patient's chronic heavy intake places him in the enzyme-induced, higher-risk group.

optionExplanations.b: Inhibition of CYP2E1 occurs with acute alcohol ingestion and reduces rather than increases toxic metabolite formation.
optionExplanations.c: CYP1A2 induction is associated with smoking and affects drugs such as theophylline and clozapine.
optionExplanations.d: P-glycoprotein is a multidrug efflux pump that opposes absorption and enhances elimination of its substrates.
optionExplanations.e: Glomerular filtration is a passive process for free drug and is not the mechanism of acetaminophen hepatotoxicity.

source.reference: CP6 — Factors Affecting Drug Biotransformation: Alcohol and Enzyme Induction

questions.question: A 70-year-old man is admitted with a symptomatic tachyarrhythmia and requires therapeutic amiodarone concentrations promptly. The drug has a long elimination half-life, and calculations show that using the ordinary maintenance dose alone would take several weeks to reach steady-state. Which dosing strategy is most appropriate?

options.text: Give a loading dose, then continue the usual maintenance dose
Give the usual maintenance dose and measure a serum level after one half-life
Double the maintenance dose indefinitely
Convert the maintenance dose to a continuous infusion
Halve the dosing interval and continue indefinitely

questions.explanation: Drugs with first-order kinetics require approximately four to five half-lives to reach steady-state with repeated dosing. A loading dose is used for drugs with a long half-life and/or when there is a clinical need to rapidly achieve therapeutic levels, with amiodarone, digoxin, and phenytoin given as examples; parenteral administration is the most common way of giving a large dose to fill up the volume of distribution.

optionExplanations.b: Therapeutic drug monitoring is of greatest utility once steady-state has been reached, which takes about four to five half-lives.
optionExplanations.c: Persistently doubling the maintenance dose would produce a supratherapeutic steady-state concentration rather than simply reaching target faster safely.
optionExplanations.d: Continuous infusion is used for drugs with a very short half-life when repeated dosing is impractical, such as nitroprusside or unfractionated heparin.
optionExplanations.e: Shortening the dosing interval indefinitely also raises the eventual steady-state concentration rather than providing a defined loading strategy.

source.reference: CP7 — Steady-State Drug Concentration / Loading and Maintenance Doses

questions.question: An 82-year-old woman with declining renal function is reviewed on the ward. Her medications include several long-standing agents that have never been adjusted for her age or renal function. Her physician wishes to use serum drug concentrations to optimize dosing for the medication most likely to require this approach. Which drug is it?

options.text: Digoxin
Amlodipine
Atorvastatin
Ramipril
Metformin

questions.explanation: Therapeutic drug monitoring uses serum drug concentration data to optimize therapy and is reserved for drugs with low therapeutic indices, unpredictable dose-response relationships, serious consequences of failure or toxicity, and wide interpatient pharmacokinetic variability; most drugs do not require it. Digoxin is explicitly listed among the drugs that sometimes require therapeutic drug monitoring, alongside vancomycin, aminoglycosides, phenytoin and other anticonvulsants, warfarin, and lithium.

optionExplanations.b: Amlodipine is not among the drugs listed as sometimes requiring therapeutic drug monitoring.
optionExplanations.c: Atorvastatin is not a low therapeutic index drug requiring serum concentration monitoring.
optionExplanations.d: Ramipril is monitored clinically and biochemically rather than by serum drug concentration.
optionExplanations.e: Metformin is described as a weak base handled by tubular secretion, but it is not listed as a therapeutic drug monitoring agent.

questions.question: A 76-year-old man with heart failure takes ramipril and spironolactone. He develops dysuria and is prescribed a seven-day course of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Three days later he reports malaise and is found to have a new conduction abnormality on ECG. Which adverse consequence of this drug combination is most likely responsible?

options.text: Hyperkalemia
Rhabdomyolysis
Serotonin syndrome
Supratherapeutic INR with bleeding
Profound hypotension

questions.explanation: Sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim combined with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or spironolactone carries an increased risk of hyperkalemia. The mechanism is pharmacodynamic: trimethoprim reduces renal potassium excretion by inhibiting sodium channels in the distal tubule, which decreases sodium reabsorption. This patient is on two agents that already impair potassium excretion, so adding trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the most likely cause.

optionExplanations.b: Rhabdomyolysis is described with HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors combined with niacin, gemfibrozil, erythromycin, or itraconazole.
optionExplanations.c: Serotonin syndrome is described with SSRIs combined with St. John's wort or with selegiline and non-selective MAO inhibitors.
optionExplanations.d: An increased warfarin effect occurs when warfarin is combined with agents including trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, but this patient is not on warfarin.
optionExplanations.e: Marked hypotension is the listed consequence of combining sildenafil with nitrates.

source.reference: CP11 — Examples of Clinically Relevant Drug Interactions

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman receiving an analgesic by intravenous infusion is transitioned to the same drug given orally. To maintain comparable plasma concentrations, the oral dose prescribed must be several times larger than the intravenous dose. Absorption of the drug from the small intestine is documented to be essentially complete, and her plasma albumin is normal. Which of the following best explains the reduced bioavailability of the oral formulation?

options.text: Metabolism of the drug in the gut wall and liver before it reaches the systemic circulation
Increased binding of the drug to albumin and a1-acid glycoprotein in plasma
Reduced total surface area available for absorption across the small intestinal villi
Conversion of the drug to its non-ionized form in the acidic gastric compartment
Uptake of the drug by solute carrier (SLC) superfamily transporters in the intestinal epithelium

questions.explanation: Bioavailability (F) is the proportion of a dose that reaches the systemic circulation in an unchanged state; an IV dose has 100% bioavailability (F=1). The first-pass effect is metabolism (biotransformation) of the drug prior to reaching the systemic circulation, occurring in the GI tract and then in the liver via the portal vein after PO administration, and it reduces F. Because absorption here is complete, presystemic clearance by first-pass metabolism is the explanation for the larger oral dose requirement.

optionExplanations.b: Plasma protein binding affects the free versus bound equilibrium and distribution after the drug is in the blood; it does not determine the proportion of an oral dose reaching the systemic circulation.
optionExplanations.c: The small intestinal villi provide a large surface area and are the primary site of absorption for most orally-administered drugs, and absorption in this patient is stated to be complete.
optionExplanations.d: Non-ionized (uncharged) forms cross cell membranes more readily by passive diffusion than ionized forms, so this would favour absorption rather than reduce bioavailability.
optionExplanations.e: Members of the SLC superfamily generally function as uptake drug transporters, which would enhance rather than oppose drug absorption; efflux by P-glycoprotein, not SLC uptake, opposes absorption.

source.reference: CP4 — Pharmacokinetics: Bioavailability and First-Pass Effect

questions.question: A 41-year-old man maintained on high-dose morphine for chronic pain is transitioned to buprenorphine. Despite stepwise escalation of the buprenorphine dose, his analgesic response plateaus well below the effect he previously obtained with morphine, and he reports no further benefit from additional increments. Measured plasma buprenorphine concentrations are above the expected range. Which property of buprenorphine at the opioid receptor best explains this ceiling in response?

options.text: It is a partial agonist that elicits only a partial effect irrespective of its concentration at the receptor
It is a reversible competitive antagonist, so increasing concentrations of agonist can overcome the inhibition
It is an irreversible competitive antagonist that forms a covalent bond with the receptor and cannot be displaced
It is a non-competitive antagonist binding an alternate site distinct from the active site, producing allosteric effects
It is a full agonist with lower affinity than morphine but equal efficacy at the receptor

questions.explanation: Full agonists such as methadone or morphine can elicit a maximal effect at the opioid receptor, whereas buprenorphine is a partial agonist that can only elicit a partial effect irrespective of the concentration at the receptor, also known as a ceiling effect (i.e. reduced efficacy compared to full agonists). This is why escalating the dose and achieving high plasma concentrations does not reproduce the maximal response seen with morphine.

optionExplanations.b: A reversible competitive antagonist binds non-covalently so increasing concentrations of agonist can overcome it (e.g. naloxone versus morphine); this predicts a surmountable effect, not a plateau, and buprenorphine is producing analgesia rather than blocking it.
optionExplanations.c: Irreversible competitive antagonists form a covalent bond with the receptor and cannot be displaced, blocking other substrates from binding; this would abolish rather than partially produce an analgesic response.
optionExplanations.d: A non-competitive antagonist (negative allosteric modulator) binds an alternate site distinct from the active site and reduces the ability of the agonist to bind, as with phenoxybenzamine at adrenergic receptors; this describes antagonism, not the partial response seen here.
optionExplanations.e: A full agonist can elicit a maximal effect at the receptor; low affinity would be surmounted by the high concentrations already achieved, so it cannot explain a plateau below the morphine response.

source.reference: CP8 — Effects of Drugs on Receptors

questions.question: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department with several days of vomiting and diarrhea. She is lethargic, tachycardic, and poorly perfused, and requires immediate fluids and medications. Repeated attempts at peripheral intravenous access by two experienced clinicians have failed. Which of the following routes of drug administration is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intraosseous
Intramuscular
Subcutaneous
Rectal
Intranasal

questions.explanation: The intraosseous (IO) route is described as a rapid and reliable route of administration that is helpful for emergency administration of fluids and medications when vascular access has failed. This child needs immediate resuscitation and peripheral intravenous access cannot be obtained, so the IO route is indicated. Its recognized risks include cellulitis, fracture, fat embolism, osteomyelitis, compartment syndrome, and epiphyseal plate necrosis, but these do not outweigh the need for immediate access in an emergency.

optionExplanations.b: An aqueous intramuscular solution can give rapid onset of action (e.g. epinephrine for serious allergic reactions), but the route is for injections rather than emergency administration of resuscitation fluids, and it causes pain and hematoma at the site of injection.
optionExplanations.c: The subcutaneous route is an alternative to IV that offers constant, even absorption, but it generally takes smaller volumes than intramuscular injection and repeated injections risk tissue damage, so it cannot deliver emergency fluid resuscitation.
optionExplanations.d: Rectal administration is used when a patient is NPO, vomiting, or unconscious, but absorption is erratic, it is appropriate for a limited number of drugs, and approximately 50% of drug absorbed still goes through the portal system.
optionExplanations.e: The intranasal route is highly vascularized with rapid absorption and bypasses the first-pass effect, but not all drugs can be administered intranasally and it is not a route for emergency administration of fluids.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman has had chronic low back pain for 18 months with no underlying cancer. She takes acetaminophen intermittently and has not tried physiotherapy, an exercise program, or any other non-opioid pharmacotherapy. Frustrated by ongoing pain, she asks her family physician to prescribe an opioid. Which of the following is the best initial treatment?

options.text: Optimize non-opioid pharmacotherapy and non-pharmacologic therapy before any trial of opioids
Begin a trial of opioids restricted to less than 50 MME/day
Begin a trial of opioids at 50 to 90 MME/day
Begin a trial of opioids at 90 MME/day or more, then reduce the dose once pain is controlled
Begin an opioid now and plan a slow, collaborative taper to the lowest effective dose in three months

questions.explanation: When first considering therapy for patients with chronic non-cancer pain, the strong recommendation is to optimize non-opioid pharmacotherapy and non-pharmacologic therapy rather than starting a trial of opioids. This woman has had only intermittent acetaminophen and no non-pharmacologic treatment, so opioid-sparing options are far from exhausted. The dose ceilings of <90 MME/day, and ideally <50 MME/day, apply only once a decision to begin opioid therapy has properly been made.

optionExplanations.b: Restricting a starting dose to <50 MME/day is the correct ceiling if opioids are started, but starting them at all is premature before non-opioid and non-pharmacologic therapy is optimized.
optionExplanations.c: Even within the <90 MME/day limit, this exceeds the ideal starting range and still skips the required first step of optimizing non-opioid options.
optionExplanations.d: General approaches to opioid use include avoiding high doses; a starting dose of 90 MME/day or more breaches the recommended prescribed dose limit for chronic non-cancer pain.
optionExplanations.e: A slow, collaborative taper to the lowest effective dose is advised for patients already using 90 MME/day or more, not as a plan for initiating opioids in an opioid-naive patient.

questions.topic: Opioid Therapy in Chronic Non-Cancer Pain

source.reference: CP12 — Opioid Therapy and Chronic Non-Cancer Pain: General Management Principles

questions.question: A 58-year-old man with a chronic illness requiring lifelong daily therapy is about to begin treatment. He has moderate renal impairment and takes several interacting medications, so the team wants the agent least likely to cause serious toxicity at a therapeutic dose. Five agents of the same class are equally effective. Preclinical ED50 and TD50 values are given with each option. Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Agent V (ED50 2 mg, TD50 30 mg)
Agent W (ED50 10 mg, TD50 120 mg)
Agent X (ED50 25 mg, TD50 500 mg)
Agent Y (ED50 1 mg, TD50 18 mg)
Agent Z (ED50 50 mg, TD50 600 mg)

questions.explanation: The therapeutic index is TD50/ED50, a measure of relative drug safety used when comparing drugs to examine the likelihood of a therapeutic dose to cause serious toxicity or death; the larger the TI, the safer the drug. Agent X has the largest therapeutic index of the five (500/25 = 20), so at an effective dose it carries the smallest relative risk of toxicity. This matters most in this patient because interacting drugs, altered ADME and patient characteristics such as age and organ impairment can all narrow the therapeutic index further.

optionExplanations.a: Agent V has a therapeutic index of 15 (30/2), lower than agent X, so it offers a smaller margin between the effective and toxic dose.
optionExplanations.b: Agent W has a therapeutic index of 12 (120/10), one of the lowest of the five options.
optionExplanations.d: Agent Y has the smallest ED50, but potency is not safety: its therapeutic index is 18 (18/1), still below that of agent X.
optionExplanations.e: Agent Z has the largest TD50, but because its ED50 is also high its therapeutic index is only 12 (600/50).

source.reference: CP9 — Effectiveness and Safety: Therapeutic Indices

questions.question: A pharmaceutical company has completed laboratory studies of a new angiotensin receptor blocker in cells, tissues, and animals, characterizing its pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties and screening for potential toxicities. The company now plans the first human study and asks a clinical pharmacologist to advise on its design. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in this drug's clinical development?

options.text: Administration to a small number of healthy volunteers to explore pharmacokinetics and safety
Administration to a small number of patients with the target condition to determine efficacy, dose range, and pharmacokinetics
A double-blinded randomized controlled trial comparing the drug with standard of care in a large group of patients
Post-marketing surveillance with wider distribution to monitor long-term effects and detect previously unappreciated adverse drug reactions
Further study in animal organs and tissues to re-examine potential toxicities before any human exposure

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes defines phase I as the first administration of a drug to a small number of healthy volunteers, following pre-clinical studies, undertaken to explore pharmacokinetics and safety. The pre-clinical assessment in cells, tissues, and animals is already complete in this case, so the appropriate first-in-human study is a small phase I safety and pharmacokinetic study in healthy volunteers. Efficacy is not addressed until the drug is first given to patients in phase II.

optionExplanations.b: This describes phase II, the first administration of the drug to patients in small sample sizes to determine efficacy, safety, dose range, and pharmacokinetics; it follows phase I rather than preceding it.
optionExplanations.c: Comparative double-blinded randomized controlled trials against placebo or standard of care in a larger group of patients are phase III studies, undertaken only after phase I and phase II.
optionExplanations.d: Post-marketing surveillance to determine effectiveness, monitor long-term drug effects, and detect previously unappreciated adverse drug reactions is phase IV, which occurs after the drug is marketed.
optionExplanations.e: Pre-clinical assessment in cells, tissues, organs, and animals examining pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties and potential toxicities has already been completed, so repeating it does not advance development.

source.reference: CP2 — General Principles: Phases of Clinical Drug Testing

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman at 34 weeks' gestation is admitted with severe preeclampsia and is to receive intravenous magnesium sulphate for seizure prophylaxis. The resident writes a handwritten order reading "MgSO4 4 g IV now". The nurse transcribing the order prepares morphine sulphate instead, and the error is intercepted before anything is given. Which change to the way the order was written would most likely have prevented this error?

options.text: Writing the drug name out in full rather than using an abbreviation
Writing the dose as "4.0 g" rather than "4 g"
Adding a leading zero before the decimal point in the dose
Writing "unit" in full rather than using the abbreviation "U"
Using "mcg" rather than the symbol "µg" in the dose

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists abbreviations for drug names among the dangerous abbreviations, symbols, and dose designations that should never be used when communicating medication information, because similar abbreviations for multiple drugs are misinterpreted: MS and MSO4 (morphine sulphate) and MgSO4 (magnesium sulphate) may be confused for one another. The stated correction is simply not to abbreviate drug names. The transcription error here arose from exactly that confusion, so writing "magnesium sulphate" in full would most likely have prevented it.

optionExplanations.b: A trailing zero is itself listed as a dangerous dose designation: the decimal point is overlooked and a 10-fold dose error results, so "4.0 g" would add risk rather than remove it.
optionExplanations.c: A zero should always be placed before a decimal point when the dose is less than one, but this dose contains no decimal point and the misinterpretation involved the drug name.
optionExplanations.d: "U" is mistaken for "0", "4", or cc and should be written as "unit", but no units were used in this order.
optionExplanations.e: "µg" is mistaken for "mg" and should be written as "mcg", but this dose was written in grams and the confusion concerned the drug name.

source.reference: CP13 — Dangerous Abbreviations, Symbols, and Dose Designations
